entities.summary:
The Maurya Empire (322–185 BCE) was the largest empire in the Indian subcontinent, founded by Chandragupta Maurya with guidance from his minister Chanakya (Kautilya). At its peak under Emperor Ashoka, it controlled the entire Indian subcontinent except the deep south, a territory exceeding 5 million square kilometers and encompassing an estimated 50–60 million people — a third of the world's population at that time.

Chandragupta's overthrow of the Nanda dynasty and subsequent campaigns against Seleucid ruler Seleucus I Nicator — resulting in the first major treaty between Indian and Hellenistic powers — established Maurya as the subcontinent's supreme power. Chanakya's Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft and economic policy, represents one of antiquity's most sophisticated works of political theory, anticipating Machiavelli by nearly two millennia.

Emperor Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism following the bloody Kalinga War (261 BCE), where an estimated 100,000 were killed and 150,000 deported, transformed him into history's greatest example of a ruler who changed course. Ashoka's rock edicts — inscribed on stones and pillars across the empire — proclaimed policies of religious tolerance, animal welfare, and humane governance. He sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and the Hellenistic kingdoms, making Buddhism a world religion.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Maurya Empire unified the Indian subcontinent for the first time and produced Ashoka, whose Buddhist conversion and rock edicts established principles of humane governance and religious tolerance that influenced world history.
